reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Defined by the combination of multiple enchondromas with soft-tissue vascular lesions, classically spindle-cell haemangiomas
Like Ollier disease it is a sporadic, non-hereditary condition caused by somatic mosaic IDH1 or IDH2 variants
Enchondromas show an asymmetric distribution affecting the hands, feet and long bones, causing deformity, swelling and limb-length discrepancy
The vascular lesions present as compressible, sometimes bluish subcutaneous nodules and may contain phleboliths visible on radiographs
Carries a higher overall risk of malignancy than Ollier disease, including chondrosarcoma and an increased risk of other neoplasms
Associated tumours reported include gliomas, and ovarian and pancreatic neoplasms, so surveillance extends beyond the skeleton
The presence of haemangiomas is the feature that separates Maffucci syndrome from isolated enchondromatosis
reference.pathophysiology: Maffucci syndrome shares its origin with Ollier disease in post-zygotic somatic mosaic gain-of-function variants of IDH1 or IDH2. The resulting oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate perturbs epigenetic regulation, impairing chondrocyte differentiation so residual cartilage persists as intramedullary enchondromas. In Maffucci syndrome the mosaic mutation additionally affects vascular tissue, giving rise to spindle-cell haemangiomas and other vascular malformations. The broader mutational burden is thought to underlie the higher risk of malignant transformation and of non-skeletal tumours compared with Ollier disease.
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey to map enchondromas and identify phleboliths within vascular lesions
MRI to characterise both cartilaginous and vascular soft-tissue lesions
Consideration of somatic IDH1/IDH2 testing on lesional tissue where diagnosis is uncertain
Surveillance imaging for malignant transformation of enchondromas
Broader clinical vigilance and targeted imaging for associated non-skeletal tumours
redFlags: Growth or new pain in an enchondroma suggesting transformation to chondrosarcoma
Neurological symptoms that may indicate an associated intracranial tumour
A rapidly enlarging or bleeding vascular lesion
Systemic features suggesting an associated visceral neoplasm
reference.prognosis: Morbidity arises from skeletal deformity, fractures and vascular lesions, but the defining concern is a substantially increased lifetime risk of malignancy, both chondrosarcoma and other tumours, mandating lifelong multi-system surveillance.
pitfalls: Managing it as simple enchondromatosis and neglecting surveillance for the broader malignancy risk
Giving inherited recurrence-risk counselling for what is a sporadic mosaic disorder
Overlooking the vascular lesions that define the syndrome and its higher risk
Failing to investigate new neurological or systemic symptoms for associated neoplasms

Orphanet / WHO Classification of Tumours: Maffucci Syndrome
management: No medical cure exists, so management centres on surveillance for malignant transformation and treatment of complications in this somatic mosaic, non-hereditary IDH1/IDH2 disorder
Surgical treatment of symptomatic enchondromas with curettage, grafting, and correction of deformity and limb-length discrepancy
Prompt biopsy and wide surgical resection of any lesion suspicious for chondrosarcoma, such as one showing growth, new pain or cortical destruction
Management of the spindle-cell haemangiomas and other vascular lesions surgically or with sclerotherapy when symptomatic
Lifelong surveillance imaging of the skeleton for malignant transformation, with broader vigilance for associated non-skeletal tumours including gliomas and ovarian and pancreatic neoplasms
Orthopaedic and rehabilitation support for deformity, fractures and functional limitation
Multidisciplinary care through skeletal-dysplasia and oncology services
